summary: Defines the IP Authentication Header, which gives IP datagrams connectionless integrity and origin authentication, along with protection against replayed packets. It proves a packet came from who it says and was not changed on the way. It was replaced by RFC 4302 and RFC 4305.

plainLanguage.summary: AH is the IPsec header that proves a packet is genuine. It adds a code to the packet that covers the contents and also the address fields, so a reader can tell that nothing was changed on the way and that the packet really came from the host it names.

questions: what is the ip authentication header
what is the difference between ah and esp
how does ah handle ip header fields that change
how does ah prevent replay attacks
subtitle: The IPsec header that proves a packet came from where it claims and was not altered.

tldr.problem: A packet crossing the Internet can be read, altered or forged by anything along the way. IPsec needs a way to prove that a packet really came from the host it claims to come from and has not been changed.
tldr.mechanism: AH adds a header after the IP header that carries a security association identifier, a sequence number and a check value computed over the packet, including the IP header fields that cannot change in transit. The receiver recomputes the check value and rejects the packet if it does not match.
tldr.outcome: Because AH covers the IP header, it protects the addresses and other fields that ESP leaves alone, but it does not encrypt anything. The RFC replaced RFC 1826 and was later obsoleted by RFC 4302 and RFC 4305.

today: RFC 2402 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 1826 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 4302 and RFC 4305.

sections.title: What AH Provides
sections.content:
The IP Authentication Header provides connectionless integrity and data origin authentication for IP datagrams. It may be applied alone, in combination with the IP Encapsulating Security Payload, or in a nested fashion through the use of tunnel mode. Security services can be provided between a pair of communicating hosts, between a pair of communicating security gateways, or between a security gateway and a host.

ESP may be used to provide the same security services, and it also provides a confidentiality service by encrypting. The primary difference between the authentication provided by ESP and AH is the extent of the coverage. ESP does not protect any IP header fields unless those fields are encapsulated by ESP in tunnel mode. AH does protect the IP header fields that cannot be changed in transit.

The protocol header that immediately precedes the AH header contains the value 51 in its Protocol field for IPv4, or its Next Header field for IPv6 and extension headers.

The document assumes the reader is familiar with the Security Architecture document, in particular the definitions of the security services offered by AH and ESP, the concept of security associations, the ways in which AH can be used with ESP, and the key management options, which for both AH and ESP are manual keying and automated keying via IKE.
sections.plainLanguage: Both IPsec headers can prove a packet is genuine. ESP can also hide the contents. The difference is that AH also covers the addresses in the IP header, which ESP leaves in the clear.

sections.title: The Authentication Header
sections.content:
All the fields of the AH format are mandatory, so they are always present and are all included in the integrity check value computation.

The Next Header is an 8-bit field identifying the type of the payload that follows the authentication header, chosen from the set of IP protocol numbers.

The Payload Length is an 8-bit field giving the length of AH in 32-bit words minus 2. AH is an IPv6 extension header, but its length is measured in 32-bit words, so the field is calculated by subtracting 2 rather than 1. In the standard case of a 96-bit authentication value plus the fixed three-word portion, the field reads 4. A null authentication algorithm may be used only for debugging, and would give 1 for IPv4 or 2 for IPv6, since there would be no authentication data field.

The Reserved field is 16 bits and must be set to zero. It is included in the authentication data calculation but otherwise ignored by the recipient.

The Security Parameters Index is an arbitrary 32-bit value that, together with the destination IP address and the security protocol, uniquely identifies the security association for the datagram. The values from 1 through 255 are reserved by IANA for future use, and the value zero is reserved for local, implementation-specific use and must not be sent on the wire.

The Sequence Number is an unsigned 32-bit counter that increases monotonically. It is always present, even if the receiver does not enable the anti-replay service. The sender's and receiver's counters start at zero when the association is established, so the first packet has a sequence number of 1. If anti-replay is enabled, which is the default, the number must never cycle, so the counters must be reset by establishing a new association and a new key before the 2^32nd packet is sent.

The Authentication Data holds the integrity check value for the packet and must be a whole number of 32-bit words long. It may include explicit padding, which is there to make the length of the header a multiple of 32 bits in IPv4 or 64 bits in IPv6. All implementations must support such padding, and the authentication algorithm specification must state the length of the check value and the comparison rules for validation.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is short: what comes next, how long the header is, a reserved field set to zero, the number of the set of keys in use, a counter, and the check value itself. Every one of those fields is covered by the check value.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
Like ESP, AH may be employed in transport mode or tunnel mode. Transport mode is applicable only to host implementations and provides protection for upper layer protocols in addition to selected IP header fields. In transport mode AH is inserted after the IP header and before an upper layer protocol such as TCP, UDP or ICMP, or before any other IPsec headers that have already been inserted. In IPv4 that means placing AH after the IP header and any options it contains, but before the upper layer protocol. The RFC notes that the word transport should not be misconstrued as restricting the mode to TCP and UDP, and that an ICMP message may be sent using either transport mode or tunnel mode.

In IPv6, AH is viewed as an end-to-end payload, so it should appear after the hop-by-hop, routing and fragmentation extension headers. The destination options extension headers may appear either before or after the AH header, depending on the semantics wanted.

Tunnel mode AH may be used by hosts or security gateways. When AH is implemented in a security gateway to protect transit traffic, tunnel mode must be used. In tunnel mode the inner IP header carries the ultimate source and destination addresses, while an outer IP header may hold different addresses, for example the addresses of security gateways. AH protects the entire inner IP packet, including the entire inner IP header, and its position relative to the outer IP header is the same as in transport mode.

ESP and AH headers can be combined in a variety of modes, and the IPsec Architecture document describes which combinations of security associations must be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: In transport mode the header sits inside the packet, so the IP addresses stay visible but are covered by the check. In tunnel mode the whole packet is wrapped in a new one, so the original addresses are hidden inside.

sections.title: Computing the Integrity Check Value
sections.content:
The check value is computed over three things. First, the IP header fields that are either immutable in transit or whose value at the endpoint can be predicted. Second, the AH header itself, meaning the next header, payload length, reserved, SPI and sequence number fields, plus the authentication data field itself, which is set to zero for the computation, and any explicit padding bytes. Third, the upper layer protocol data, which is assumed to be immutable in transit.

Some fields may be modified during transit, and for those the value is set to zero for the purposes of the computation. A field that is mutable but whose value at the receiver is predictable has that predicted value inserted instead. The authentication data field is also set to zero. Replacing a field's value with zero rather than omitting it preserves alignment for the computation, and it also ensures that the length of the fields handled this way cannot change during transit even though their contents are not explicitly covered.

The RFC classifies the IPv4 base header fields. The immutable ones are the version, the internet header length, the total length, the identification, the protocol, the source address, and the destination address when loose or strict source routing is not used. The destination address with loose or strict source routing is mutable but predictable, so its final value is used. The fields that are mutable and zeroed are the type of service, the flags, the fragment offset, the time to live and the header checksum.

Each exclusion has a reason. The type of service is excluded because some routers are known to change it even though the IP specification does not treat it as mutable. The flags are excluded because an intermediate router might set the don't-fragment bit even if the source did not select it. The fragment offset is excluded because AH is applied only to unfragmented IP packets, so the offset must always be zero. The time to live changes in the normal course of processing and is therefore not predictable by the sender, and the header checksum changes whenever any of the other fields does.

IPv4 has no way of tagging options as mutable, so the options are listed explicitly in an appendix and classified individually. The whole option is treated as a unit, so if an option is classified as mutable the entire option is zeroed. IPv6 options carry a flag that says whether the option might change unpredictably during transit; for any option that may change, the whole option data field must be treated as zero-valued octets when computing or verifying the check value, while the option type and length are still included.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every field in an IP header stays the same on the way. A router changes the time to live and may change other fields. So those fields are set to zero before the check is calculated, and the receiver does the same, so both sides agree on what was checked.

sections.title: Receiving a Packet and the Replay Window
sections.content:
On receipt of a packet containing an authentication header, the receiver determines the appropriate unidirectional association from the destination IP address, the protocol and the SPI. The association says whether the sequence number will be checked, which algorithm to use for the check value, and which key to use. If no valid association exists, for example because the receiver has no key, the packet must be discarded, and that is an auditable event.

All AH implementations must support the anti-replay service, though the receiver may enable or disable it for each association. It must not be enabled unless the authentication service is also enabled, because otherwise the sequence number is not protected. The RFC notes that there are no provisions for managing transmitted sequence numbers among several senders directing traffic to a single association, whatever the destination address, so the anti-replay service should not be used in that situation.

If the receiver has enabled anti-replay, the receive counter starts at zero when the association is established, and each packet must carry a sequence number that has not been seen during the life of that association. This should be the first check applied after the packet is matched to an association, to speed the rejection of duplicates.

Duplicates are rejected with a sliding receive window. A minimum window size of 32 must be supported, and a size of 64 is preferred and should be the default. The receiver does not tell the sender what size it uses. The right edge of the window is the highest validated sequence number received, and packets below the left edge are rejected. Packets inside the window are checked against a list of the packets already received there. If the packet is inside the window and new, or to the right of it, the receiver proceeds to verify the check value. If that fails, the packet must be discarded as invalid, and that is an auditable event. The window is updated only if the check value verifies.

To verify, the receiver saves the check value and replaces it with zero, without touching any padding, zeroes every other field that may have changed during transit, appends zero-filled bytes if the algorithm needs the packet length padded, computes the check value and compares it with the saved one using the rules the algorithm specification defines. If they match the datagram is valid and accepted; if not, the receiver must discard it, and that too is an auditable event.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver keeps a note of the numbers it has already seen, in a sliding list of the last few dozen packets. A packet with an old number, or one it has seen before, is thrown away before any real work is done. Then the check value is recomputed and compared.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC says that security is central to the design of the protocol, so the security considerations permeate the specification, and that additional aspects of using IPsec are discussed in the Security Architecture document.

Auditing follows the same pattern as the rest of IPsec. Not every system that implements AH will implement auditing, but if AH is incorporated into a system that supports auditing then the AH implementation must also support it, and a system administrator must be able to enable or disable it. Several auditable events are identified, and for each a minimum set of information should go in the log, such as the SPI value, the date and time, the source and destination addresses and, in IPv6, the flow ID. There is no requirement for the receiver to send a message to the purported sender when it detects an auditable event, because of the potential to induce a denial of service by doing so.

Implementations claiming conformance must fully implement the AH syntax and processing described here and must comply with all the requirements of the Security Architecture document. If the key used to compute the check value is manually distributed, correct provision of the anti-replay service would need the sender to maintain its counter state carefully until the key is replaced, and there would likely be no automated recovery if the counter were about to overflow, so a compliant implementation should not provide that service for manually keyed associations. A compliant AH implementation must support HMAC with MD5 and HMAC with SHA-1.

The RFC also lists what changed from RFC 1826. The anti-replay service is now an integral, mandatory part of AH rather than a feature of a transform defined elsewhere, and carrying a sequence number to support it is required at all times. The default algorithms required for interoperability changed from keyed MD5 to HMAC with MD5 or SHA-1, for security reasons, and the list of IPv4 header fields excluded from the check value computation was expanded to include the offset and flags fields. Tunnel mode AH was only mentioned in passing in RFC 1826 and is now a mandatory feature.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC requires HMAC with MD5 or SHA-1, because the older keyed hash it replaced was not strong enough. It also insists that the anti-replay protection be built into the header itself rather than left as an option in another document.

viz.caption: The fields of the Authentication Header

items.title: Next Header
items.text: An 8-bit field saying what comes after the authentication header.

items.title: Payload Len
items.text: The length of the header in 32-bit words, minus 2.

items.title: Reserved
items.text: A 16-bit field that must be set to zero. It is covered by the check value but otherwise ignored.

items.title: Security Parameters Index
items.text: A 32-bit value that, with the destination address and the protocol, identifies the security association.

items.title: Sequence Number
items.text: A 32-bit counter that rises with every packet and is always present.

items.title: Authentication Data
items.text: The integrity check value, plus any padding needed to line the header up on a 32 or 64 bit boundary.

viz.caption: What the two IPsec headers protect

left.title: Authentication Header
left.desc: Covers the IP header fields that cannot change in transit as well as the payload. Does not encrypt anything.

right.title: Encapsulating Security Payload
right.desc: Can encrypt the payload, but leaves the IP header fields unprotected unless they are tunnelled.
